1:
The date given for the accession does not fit the other numbers, and both commentators who notice it reach for a co-regency to repair it. Gill works the arithmetic out: the king of Israel of the same name began to reign in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah, who reigned forty, so that Amaziah's own accession falls in the fourth year of Israel's king and not the second. His repair is to read the second year as the second of Amaziah's sole rule, since the son had reigned two or three years in his father's lifetime. Clarke puts the co-regency on the other side of the pair. The second year, he says, counts from the time Jehoahaz associated his son with himself on the throne of Israel, so that the figure marks the first year of that king's absolute and independent government and says nothing about Judah; he credits the solution to Calmet. Gill supplies a second synchronism for the length of the reign, that of the twenty-nine years fourteen ran alongside Israel's king, who reigned sixteen, and fifteen fell after him.

The verdict on the reign is double, and the commentators divide the praise from the reservation. Keil and Delitzsch read the twenty-nine years as governed by the same theocratic spirit as the father's, take the reservation from the parallel in Chronicles, where the comparison with the ideal king becomes a heart that was not perfect, and explain it by the idolatry into which this king, like his father before him, fell in the closing years. Ellicott notes the same paraphrase without pressing it further. Henry reads the reservation as a failure of perseverance, that the man began well and did not continue: he grants what the verse grants, attendance kept up at God's altars and attention kept up to God's word, and then draws out what the comparison with David is for, since it is not enough to do what pious predecessors did merely to keep the usage going, but the thing must be done as they did it, from the same principle of faith and devotion and with the same sincerity and resolution. Gill's reservation is the plainest of the three, that the right-doing was external at least, and belonged to the beginning of the reign.

The high places are the chapter's first standing exception, and the notes on them run from grammar to moral. Ellicott takes the connecting word, which the version renders one way here and another in the verse before, and prefers only, or save that, as marking the single thing withheld. Gill observes that the father had not taken them away either, so that the son inherited the omission rather than invented it. Henry's sentence on them is the one worth keeping, that it is hard to get clear of corruptions which, by long usage, have gained both prescription and a favourable opinion; Wesley keeps the clause about long usage and prescription and drops the rest. Henry's own arrangement puts this first of three views of the man, in the temple, on the bench and in the field, so that the failure over the high places stands as the measure of his religion before anything is said of his justice or his wars.
5:
The execution of the assassins was delayed, and the commentators disagree about what the king was waiting for. Gill makes it a matter of public feeling: the throne had to be settled, the people's affection won, the memory of the father's own idolatry and bloodshed worn off their minds, and the friends of the conspirators reduced to few or none. Clarke puts the danger in the conspirators themselves, who had considerable power and influence, so that it was hazardous to bring them to justice until the loyalty of the other officers was assured, and only then were they called to account and put to death. Ellicott asks nothing beyond the king's own position, that the clause means no more than being firmly established on the throne and feeling his power secure, and he notes that the verbs are literally smote and smitten rather than slew and slain.

The sparing of the children is the one act in the reign that all four praise without reserve. Gill calls it an instance of clemency and of strict regard both to justice and to the law of God, and allows that the king might have feared these very sons would one day avenge their fathers. Clarke grounds it in the same statute, that the fathers shall not be put to death for the children nor the children for the fathers, but every man shall be put to death for his own sin. Keil and Delitzsch add the historical point that the eastern custom of the time ran the other way, and that what was commonly done in the East was very likely often enough done in Israel as well. Wesley names the virtue required, faith and courage to obey a command of God at a known hazard to himself.

The Edomite campaign is told twice over, since both of the fuller commentators go to Chronicles for what this verse leaves out. Gill has an army of three hundred thousand picked men of Judah, with a hundred thousand hired out of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, dismissed again at a prophet's word, after which the ten thousand slain were matched by ten thousand taken alive and thrown headlong from a rock. Clarke tells the same story and keeps the detail that makes it human, the king's regret for his hundred talents and the answer that the Lord could give him much more than that. Keil and Delitzsch supply the sequel the others omit, that the dismissed mercenaries were so enraged that they plundered several cities of Judah on their way home and put many men to death. On the place-names the three work in different directions. Ellicott identifies the valley of salt as the salt plain at the end of the Dead Sea, which the army would cross on its march, and Selah as the crag, the Hebrew name of the rock-hewn capital; he reads the words rendered by war as in the battle, after which the troops forced the narrow defile to the city and probably met no great resistance. Clarke reaches the same identification from the other end, that Selah or Petra gave its name to Arabia Petraea and must have had the precipice from which the captives were thrown. The new name is the one point of real division: Wesley takes Joktheel to signify the obedience of God, given as the reward of obeying the prophet's message, while Ellicott prefers God's ward, with reference to the natural strength of the site, and reports the alternative subjugated of God. Ellicott also fixes the limit of the phrase unto this day, which reaches only to the time when the document the writer drew on was composed, and he adds the irony that the gods carried off from the conquered country afterwards proved a snare to the conqueror.
8:
What the challenge was for is the first question, and three answers are offered. Gill and Clarke both ground it in redress: the hundred thousand dismissed mercenaries had kept their pay, fallen on the cities of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon while the king was away, killed three thousand, and Clarke adds that Amaziah remonstrated to no purpose before declaring war. Gill allows two further motives, an old grudge against the house of Jehu, and a hope of reducing the ten tribes to the house of David. Ellicott makes that second motive the real one, that the king was intoxicated by his recent success and aimed at nothing less than recovering the Ten Tribes, and he cites Josephus for the letters said to have passed between them. Keil and Delitzsch separate the outward reason from the inward ground: the raid was the pretext, but the cause was a pride that had so far carried him away that he brought home the gods of Edom and worshipped them, and threatened the prophet who condemned it into silence. Henry allows no cause at all, that the man challenged without so much as showing a quarrel, and so proved himself proud, presumptuous and prodigal of blood, since a personal duel would have kept the error with the challenger, where this brought thousands into the field.

The reply is a fable, and the commentators divide over how far it should be decoded. Clarke translates every term: the thistle is Amaziah, the cedar is Jehoash, the daughter asked for is a part of the kingdom, and the wild beast is the Israelite army that trod the thistle down. Wesley reads it the same way and adds the tone, a low and contemptible yet troublesome shrub asking of a tree far stronger, with the warning that his soldiers would tread Judah down as easily. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the point-by-point reading and keep only the figure, that a thorn-bush setting itself on an equality with a cedar represents a proud man overrating his strength and asking what passes his condition. Ellicott works the words instead, offering bramble or briar for the thistle, noting that the Syriac makes it a blackthorn, and correcting the singular beast that passes by into wild beasts that passed over it. His summary is that the difference between the two kingdoms in strength, and the disdainful tolerance of the stronger, could hardly have been put more forcibly. Henry hears in it the pride on both sides, the ancient house of David reckoned not worthy to be named the same day with the upstart house of Jehu, and observes how a humble man may smile to hear two scornful men set their wits to work to undervalue one another.

The closing counsel is read for its philology and for its justice. Ellicott renders the advice literally as be honoured and abide in thine own house, that is, rest content with the glory won, and turns the last clause into a question about provoking disaster rather than meddling to one's hurt. Wesley and Henry both take it as a warning against ambition, Henry adding that many would have had honour enough if they had known when they had enough. On the fairness of it Clarke parts company with everyone: he finds the answer full of insolent dignity and empty of any offer of amends, calls the raid base and cowardly, since it fell on women, old men and children while the fighting men were in Edom, and holds Amaziah's quarrel certainly just. His explanation of the defeat is therefore not military but moral, that the gods of Seir which the king had set up and burnt incense to delivered him into his enemy's hand. Gill reaches the same end more shortly, that the pride behind the message went before a fall.
11:
The refusal to listen is referred to God, and the battlefield is placed. Gill makes the deafness judicial, a hardness of heart given over by an overruling providence so that he might be punished for setting up the gods of Edom and offering to them. Ellicott puts the encounter in the great plain north of Beth-shemesh, the modern Ain-shems, and reads looking one another in the face here as simply joining battle; he adds that Jehoash meant to come at Jerusalem from the west, as Hazael had intended before him. How Judah lost is the first real difference. Gill and Wesley both take the account from Josephus, that a sudden terror seized them so that they never struck a stroke but every man made the best of his way before the lines closed. Ellicott reads the same clause as a plain military formula, that they went off to their tents in the sense that the beaten army disbanded, as armies usually did after a great defeat;

The capture of the king is the detail the commentators dwell on, and Ellicott's note is the longest in the chapter. He observes that the formal recital of Amaziah's descent, which Thenius took for a mark that this narrative came from the northern annals, at least shows the weight the writer put on the incident. He prefers the reading that Jehoash brought him a prisoner to his own capital, and renders the next clause as making a breach rather than breaking the wall down, since no resistance appears to have been offered. Josephus he will not follow in making Amaziah open the gates under menace of death, which he calls a needless assumption when the army was already routed and the king taken; the chariot driven through the breach with the prisoner behind it he lets stand. His topography is exact: the gate of Ephraim on the north, also called the gate of Benjamin and answering to the modern Damascus gate, the corner gate at the north-west angle, and four hundred cubits as about two hundred and twenty yards. For the motive he offers the insolence of a victor and a forcible way of teaching Amaziah that his strongest city was no proof against Ephraim, with Thenius wanting room for a triumphal entry. Gill's comment is the driest, that the two now looked one another in the face indeed, and that one of them must have looked very silly, while Wesley thinks the pedigree is dragged in because the man was smarting for his ancestors' iniquity.

What was taken, and on what terms it ended, divides the last two voices. Gill notes from Chronicles that the temple treasure had been in the keeping of Obededom's family, who held the charge by lot. Ellicott hears a hint in the phrase that the gold and silver were what was found, as though there were not much left to carry off, and he reads the hostages as the sons of sureties, taken for good behaviour by a victor who had humbled his pride and left him on his throne; the Assyrian kings of Sargon's line, he adds, record the same sort of clemency of themselves. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the throne was never lost, since the man reigned fifteen years after the death of the king who captured him. Clarke assumes the opposite, that Amaziah got his liberty afterwards but how or on what terms is not known, and that the pledges were probably nobles or members of his own family given to buy it back, to be released when he had performed engagements we know nothing of. Keil and Delitzsch close with the chapter's bookkeeping, that the notice of Jehoash's death is given twice, and argue from the older spelling of his name here that the writer was copying the annals as he found them.
15:
The death notice has been given once already, and the commentators account for its coming round again. Henry observes that the funeral was attended earlier in the book, and that the historian repeats the death and the burial because he had more of the man's life and actions to set down first. Gill fills out the formula on either side, taking the might to mean the valiant acts of the Syrian wars and the sleeping with his fathers to mean no more than that he died as they died. Clarke deflates the other half of the formula: for all that is said about how he fought with Amaziah, the only fighting between them was the one battle, and the full account of it is in Chronicles. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the two facts the verse adds, the burial in Samaria among the kings of Israel and the succession of a son who bore the name of the first king of the north.

Henry's note here surveys all three of the deaths this part of the chapter records, and his judgements on the other two are worth having in advance. Of Amaziah he remarks that fifteen years of survival after a public humiliation show how a man may live a great while after he has been shamed, and be thoroughly mortified without being dead. He makes something of what the annals are said to contain, since the acts are there but the might is not, and he holds that a man cruel to the beaten Edomites and insolent to the king of Israel had shown himself void of true courage. He traces the conspiracy to maladministration, with the broken wall of Jerusalem a standing reproach that the king's own folly and presumption had brought on the city, so that his subjects hated him and the capital grew too hot to hold him. Of the son he notices the long gap, that Amaziah died in the fifteenth year of the northern king while the boy did not begin to reign until the twenty-seventh, since he was four years old when his father was killed and the government stayed in the hands of protectors for twelve years until he was sixteen. His last observation is on the historian's manner rather than the history, that a reign which ran very long is gathered up here in a single building project and then broken off.
17:
The fifteen years are checked against the other numbers and found to fit. Gill adds them to the fourteen that ran alongside the northern king to make the twenty-nine of the regnal formula, and records that the Latin version reads twenty-five instead. Ellicott runs the same sum from the accession in the second year of a king who reigned sixteen, pronounces the data self-consistent, and draws one inference from them, that the victor died very soon after his victory, perhaps in the following year. On the formula about the annals Gill enters the distinction that matters, that the book referred to is not the canonical Chronicles, where some things about this king are recorded that are not here, but the yearly record kept for each reign by a historian appointed for the purpose.

What raised the conspiracy is the chapter's last real question, and the answers differ in kind. Gill names the conspirators as the principal men of Jerusalem, and suggests that those whose sons had been carried off as hostages laid that loss, with the broken wall and the stripping of temple and palace, to the king's bad management. Clarke makes the same causes general, that the defeat, the pillaged temple, the emptied exchequer and the dismantled city had left him so unpopular that the whole of his last fifteen years were probably a series of troubles and distresses. Ellicott argues instead from the silence of the record, since no individual conspirators are named, which points to a general disaffection rather than a plot; Thenius he reports as supposing some particular act that incensed the army, and he allows that the ill-fated enterprise against Israel had probably something to do with it. The flight itself he reads as evidence, that running to Lachish, once a strong fortress and now Um Lâkis, suggests either a popular rising in the capital or a military revolt, and that the sending of men after him points the same way.

How the body came home is disputed down to the preposition. Keil and Delitzsch understand a hearse to which the king's own horses had been harnessed, and keep the burial in the royal tomb with his fathers. Ellicott offers two possibilities, the royal chariot in which the king had fled, or a corpse carried literally on horseback by the men who killed him, and then turns the manner of it into an argument: the orderly proceeding, the burial in the royal sepulchres and the raising of the son to the throne together seem to prove that this was no act of private blood-revenge. Gill reports the Jewish reading, that the horses were a judgment answering to the offence, since a king who had worshipped gods that were themselves carried on horses was not to be carried on the shoulders of men, that honour belonging to the service he had neglected.
21:
Who put the boy on the throne is the first point of difference. Keil and Delitzsch insist on the plain sense, that all the people of Judah means the whole nation and not the men of war, which is how Thenius had read it. Ellicott reports that reading without dismissing it, and finds a further hint in the verb: being taken suggests that this son was not the eldest, since a father who died at fifty-nine probably had sons older than sixteen, so that the choice fell on a popular or perhaps a military favourite. Against both stands Wesley's note, that the thing was not done until twelve years after the father's death, the government resting until then in the hands of protectors. Keil and Delitzsch leave no room for such an interval, since on their reading the new king fortified Elath immediately after his accession, and Ellicott calls him a warlike youth who took the field at once.

The double name is a smaller puzzle that two of the four refuse to treat as one. Gill and Clarke are content to observe that Azariah and Uzziah come to much the same thing, the help of the Lord and the strength of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch will not have it so cheaply: the two forms are distributed too consistently across the historical books and the prophets to be put down to a copyist, and neither the guess that the king adopted the second name on his accession nor the guess that the soldiers gave it to him after a campaign accounts for the way the books actually use them. Ellicott inclines to the accession-name, admits that which of the two was taken up cannot be said, and brings a parallel from Assyria, where Sennacherib renamed Esarhaddon on investing him with the sovereignty.

The one act recorded of the new reign is read as the completion of his father's war. Gill traces the port through its whole history, Edomite at first, probably taken by David when he made that people tributary, retaken at the revolt, recovered by Amaziah, and now rebuilt and fortified. Clarke places it on the eastern arm of the Red Sea, which takes its name of Elanitic Gulf from the town, and supposes it had suffered badly in the late war before being brought wholly under Judah. Keil and Delitzsch read the work as evidence that the son finished the subjugation of Edom which the father had begun, and explain why the notice stands here, before anything is said of the length or character of the reign, by the importance of a work that both marked its opening and showed its power. Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun, he built, in contrast with his father, and builds a conjecture on it: the father may have let the conquest slacken after his defeat, may even have lost ground to Edom, and that, Thenius suggested, could be what raised the conspiracy against him. On the closing clause, that this followed after the king slept with his fathers, Ellicott grants that Thenius explains it better than anyone and still finds it surprising where it stands.
23:
The forty-one years will not reconcile with the rest of the book. Keil and Delitzsch observe that a son who came to the throne only in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah cannot be fitted to a reign of forty-one; Thenius would read fifty-one and Ewald fifty-three. Ellicott reaches fifty-one by addition, fourteen years alongside Amaziah and thirty-seven alongside Azariah, and traces the lower figure to a confusion of two Hebrew letters. Henry takes the number as it stands and draws a moral, that the longest reign in the north was exactly the length of Asa's, though one of those two did good and the other evil, so that character cannot be measured by length of life. On the evil itself Henry presses the plea the king would have offered, that the calves had been the way of all his ancestors, and answers that a sin is none the less evil for being an ancient usage. Keil and Delitzsch grant in one breath that he held firmly to that image-worship and raised his kingdom again to great power.

The recovered border is measured from both ends. Keil and Delitzsch take it from the approach to Hamath in the north to the sea of the Arabah, the limits the kingdom had under Solomon, and think the Pentateuch's name for the southern boundary was the prophet's own. Ellicott makes the northern point the frontier of the Hamathite territory, the limit originally appointed for Israel and the one Ezekiel names for the future, reached before this only under Solomon, and at the other end includes the whole length of the Dead Sea and the country beyond Jordan; his emphatic rendering also puts the agency beyond doubt, that it was this king who wrested the land back out of Syrian hands. Clarke measures the gain rather than the line, that the whole territory taken from the kings of Israel was reconquered, leaving the kingdom as ample as when the ten tribes first separated.

The prophet who foretold it draws the most varied comment in the chapter. Ellicott places his birthplace at the modern Meshed north of Nazareth, reports Ewald's remark that a man whom tradition connects with Nineveh must have worked a very wide field, and weighs the proposal of Hitzig and Knobel that the prophecy survives in two chapters of Isaiah, though he judges it easier to show those chapters are not Isaiah's than that they are Jonah's. Clarke holds the opposite, that the prophecy delivered on this occasion is not extant, since the book bearing the man's name deals wholly with Nineveh. Henry makes the Galilean birth tell against those who said no prophet arises out of Galilee, and reads the commission as evidence of pardon, since a messenger who had himself fled and fretted was afterwards sent with mercy to Israel.

Why a kingdom in this condition was helped is answered the same way throughout. Gill and Wesley make the oppression the ground of the pity, an unworthy people left with nothing shut up, nothing left and no helper, and Clarke adds that the calamity fell on all alike, the diseased and the dungeon prisoners with the rest. Keil and Delitzsch find the words taken verbatim from the song of Moses, to show that the nation had come to the exact extremity foretold there, and gloss the next verse as meaning that the sentence of rejection had not yet been uttered through any prophet. Ellicott prefers oppression to affliction and stubborn to bitter, and on the figure of blotting out notes that Hebrew inks faded and could be wiped from the parchment. Gill and Henry differ over the force of the reprieve: Gill has the sentence pronounced later by Hosea and executed in the reign of Hoshea, while Henry holds that the name was never blotted out, since it survives in the gospel Israel.
28:
The recovery of Damascus and Hamath is the chapter's hardest clause, and the two who work it reach opposite kinds of answer. Clarke explains it from history: David had conquered all Syria, garrisoned Damascus and laid the Syrians under tribute, after which they threw off the yoke and took a considerable part of Israel's territory for themselves, so that what this king won back had belonged to Judah by David's conquests and was now annexed to the north. Ellicott finds the words themselves out of joint. He takes the two names for portions of territory rather than the whole independent states, reads the qualifying phrase as restrictive, so that the sense is Judæan Damascus and Hamath, and admits that the following words, which in Hebrew say in Israel rather than for Israel, are obscure. He reports Ewald's remedy, striking out the reference to Judah and reading Israel with the Syriac and Arabic, but notes that the Greek, the Latin and the Targum all support the text as it stands; another way out makes the restoration to Judah as the theocratic people and through Israel as the kingdom that actually annexed the districts. His verdict is that no explanation is really satisfactory, and his own guess is an editor's slip, Judah written for Israel, with a marginal note afterwards creeping into the text. Ellicott also supplies the political setting, that this reign ran alongside an Assyrian king whose own records claim tribute from Tyre and Sidon, from the land of Omri, from Edom and Philistia, and a siege of Damascus that ended in its king's submission and the spoiling of his palace, so that the lasting success of a man who was himself an Assyrian vassal rests on the prostration of his enemy by somebody else. Gill, for his part, reads the formula as it stands, that the acts were valiant and the exploits warlike.

The succession is the last disagreement, and it turns on a number. Clarke has an orderly transfer, a natural death and a regular succession by a son who reigned badly, was killed after six months, and began the sequence of one-month and ten-year reigns that followed; the interregnum his margin pointed to he cannot account for in any satisfactory way. Keil and Delitzsch show why an interregnum is wanted: a reign of forty-one years puts this death in the twenty-seventh year of Uzziah, and a son who did not begin to reign until the thirty-eighth cannot have taken the throne when his father left it. Clarke adds the one incident of the reign preserved outside the annals, that Amos, who prophesied in these years, was accused by an idolatrous priest of Beth-el of predicting the king's death by the sword, which was a slander, since what he did predict is in his own book and came to pass. Wesley makes the reign a landmark in another way, as the time when Hosea began to prophesy and became the first to write his prophecies, with Amos alongside him, Micah soon after and Isaiah in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah, so that the darkest age of the church was given burning and shining lights, a few of whom wrote and so throw their light forward.
